title: Manthara
hook: a maid on a rooftop sees the lights, and the first person she tells is overjoyed
carry: I see no difference between them

segments.voice: Yesterday: abhisheka, and the city lit up for it, you are my second self. Lamps in the trees, waters ready for the pouring. Did you tell someone a good thing was theirs too? Today, someone on a rooftop. Day five hundred seventeen.

Valmiki doesn't tell us much about where she came from. She is a maid from Queen Kaikeyi's family household, and she has always lived beside Kaikeyi. Her name is Manthara. The text says her back is bent. On the night before the coronation, she happens to climb up to a high terrace, the way anyone might go up to the roof to see what the noise is about. And below her, the whole city is glowing.
screen: `A MAID FROM KAIKEYI'S FAMILY.` → `UP TO THE ROOF.` → `THE CITY IS GLOWING.`

segments.voice: Manthara sees banners, flowers, people in their best clothes, music in the streets. She turns to a nurse standing nearby. What's going on? Why is Kausalya, Rama's mother, handing out gifts? The nurse, delighted, tells her: tomorrow the king will make Rama his heir. Manthara goes down the stairs in a fury. She finds Kaikeyi lying on her bed and tells her to get up. Something terrible is happening to you, she says, and you're lying there. The king is going to make Rama heir. Your good fortune is about to dry up like a river in summer. And here is the first surprise. Kaikeyi is glad. Truly glad. She sits up, delighted, and gives Manthara a beautiful jewel as a reward for the news. Then she says the line that matters most for everything that follows. Rama and Bharata are the same to me. I see no difference between them. If Rama is made king, what better news could you bring me? Hold onto that. Before anyone whispers anything, Kaikeyi loves Rama. She's happy for him. Quick retellings often make Kaikeyi the wicked stepmother from her first scene. Valmiki doesn't write her that way. He lets us see her generous first, so that when she changes, we see the change happen. That's why the story stays uncomfortable. The person who will send Rama away is not a stranger and not a monster. She's someone who loved him an hour ago. Manthara has heard all this. And she throws the jewel on the floor.
screen: `WHAT'S GOING ON DOWN THERE?` · `MANTHARA RUSHES TO KAIKEYI.` · `KAIKEYI IS GLAD, AND GIVES A JEWEL.` · `I SEE NO DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THEM.` · then, large: `SHE THROWS THE JEWEL DOWN.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of a moment when someone brought you news about another person: a promotion, an engagement, a win. Remember your very first reaction, before any second thoughts arrived. Was it gladness? Let that first reaction come back, and rest in it for a few breaths. If second thoughts arrived later, just notice that they came after. The bell holds the time.
Manthara. Kaikeyi's maid, who sees the coronation lights from a rooftop and brings the news, and whose mistress is, at first, simply glad.
Your line: I see no difference between them. Today, when you hear someone else's good news, notice your very first feeling, and say it out loud if it's gladness. Day five hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Manthara's name is sometimes used for someone who stirs up trouble in a family, but the Ayodhya Kanda is read closely enough that Kaikeyi's first, generous reaction is often pointed out.

fork.setup: you're Kaikeyi. your maid rushes in: the king will make Rama heir tomorrow. what do you feel first?
fork.reveal: Kaikeyi is delighted, gives Manthara a jewel, and says she sees no difference between Rama and Bharata.

original.note: Sanskrit mantharā, the maid's name. the adjective manthara can mean slow or bent.

trapdoor: what you thought: Kaikeyi was the wicked stepmother all along.
what it means: in Valmiki, her first reaction to Rama's coronation is joy and a gift.
what a scholar hears: the text lets us watch Kaikeyi change over a few sargas, which is part of why commentators and retellers have argued for centuries about how much blame she carries.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 7 (Manthara on the terrace; Kaikeyi's joy and gift)

notes: Sarga number follows the common (vulgate) numbering; confirm.
Manthara described as a maid of Kaikeyi's family 'of unknown origin' in some readings of Ayodhya 7.1; the script says only that Valmiki tells us little. Confirm.
Her bent back (kubja): the script mentions it once, neutrally. A Keeper may prefer to drop it.
Meaning of the adjective manthara (slow, bent): confirm against a standard dictionary (Monier-Williams).

Editor review (2026-10-01): 'came with Kaikeyi when she married' is not in Ayodhya 7, which says only that she is a family servant who has always lived with Kaikeyi; corrected in voice and myth. 'Many people remember' and 'in many Hindu homes' softened.
